qs.stem: A drug is given by intravenous bolus injection and is described by a one-compartment open model. What does the model assume happens to the dose?

options.t: All of it enters at once and distributes uniformly
options.why: The bolus puts the whole dose in at once, and the one-compartment assumption spreads it evenly through the body at the same instant. Dr. Mosley adds that this does not actually happen: the model is a simplification, the simplest way to describe distribution and elimination. Elimination starts the moment the drug is in.

options.t: All of it enters at once and then distributes over several hours
options.why: A distribution step that takes measurable time is what forces a second compartment, so describing one is describing the two-compartment model instead. The one-compartment model has no distribution phase at all; the drug is uniform from time zero. Choosing this means holding the instantaneous input but not the instantaneous distribution.

options.t: It enters at a constant rate and distributes uniformly
options.why: Picking this reads the input as an infusion. Constant-rate input is intravenous infusion, a zero-order process at the input end that belongs to a later module. The word bolus fixes the input as instantaneous, the whole dose in at time zero, so attaching a rate to it replaces the mode of administration the question names.

options.t: It enters at once and stays in the plasma until elimination begins
options.why: This adds a waiting period before elimination starts, which the model does not have. Dr. Mosley says that as soon as the drug is in the body it starts immediately being eliminated. Confining the dose to plasma also confuses the plasma sample with the volume of distribution.

list: The one-compartment open model makes two simplifications, both at time zero.
Instantaneous input: the amount in the body at time zero is the whole dose.
Instantaneous, uniform distribution: one measured plasma concentration describes the whole body. This is a simplification: it holds in the model, not in the patient.
"Open" means drug can leave, and it starts leaving from that same instant.
So C0 = {{frac:D0|VD}} (D0 is the dose, VD the apparent volume of distribution), and C = C0e^(−kt) only falls from there.

qs.quote: the drug goes into the body all at once, like instantly all the drug is into the body and all the drug is instantly uniformly distributed throughout the body. Assumptions, simplifications, this does not happen.

qs.stem: Which of the following does the one-compartment open model for intravenous bolus administration assume? Select all that apply.

options.t: The body behaves as a single uniform compartment
options.why: The body acts like a single, uniform compartment, which is what allows one plasma concentration to stand for the whole body. Uniform is the operative word: no region holds a different concentration from any other.

options.t: Drug can both enter and leave the body
options.why: This is what open means in the model name. A closed compartment would retain everything put into it; the open model has an exit, and the differential equation {{frac:dDB|dt}} = −kDB describes that exit as first order in the amount present.

options.t: Input of the dose is instantaneous
options.why: Dr. Mosley calls this instantaneous input of drug into the body, and it is what distinguishes a bolus from an infusion. It sets the amount in the body at time zero equal to the full dose, which is the starting point for every calculation in this module.

options.t: Input of the dose occurs at a constant rate
options.why: Picking this reads the input as an infusion. A constant rate of input is the zero-order input of an intravenous infusion, which belongs to Module 3; a bolus places the whole dose in the body at time zero, so the amount at time zero is the dose itself.

options.t: Elimination begins only after distribution is complete
options.why: There is nothing for elimination to wait for, because distribution is instantaneous in this model. The idea of waiting for distribution is imported from the two-compartment model, where a distribution phase genuinely precedes the elimination phase on the curve.

list: Three assumptions define the model, and each does a separate job.
Instantaneous input fixes the starting amount: the whole dose.
A single uniform compartment lets one measured plasma concentration represent the whole body.
Open means elimination runs the whole time, from time zero.
A wrong statement often keeps two of the assumptions and changes the third.

qs.quote: Assumes that the drug can enter and leave the body. Body acts like a single, uniform compartment

qs.stem: What does the apparent volume of distribution of a drug represent?

options.t: A hypothetical volume that would hold the whole dose
options.why: It is the hypothetical volume of body fluid needed to dissolve the total amount of drug at the concentration found in the blood. Because it is hypothetical, the number can exceed total body water, which no real volume can. Dr. Mosley says it is not an actual volume and that it depends on the drug.

options.t: The total volume of blood and extracellular fluid present
options.why: Picking this reads an apparent volume as an anatomical one. Blood and extracellular fluid are physiological volumes of a few litres, the same for every drug, whereas VD (apparent volume of distribution) varies with the drug. A drug held almost entirely in tissue has a VD far larger than any body fluid space.

options.t: The volume of plasma completely cleared of drug each hour
options.why: That is the definition of clearance, and swapping the two is easy because both are quoted in units of volume. Clearance carries a time in its units and the volume of distribution does not, so checking whether the unit has a per-hour on it separates them immediately.

options.t: The volume of the dosage form administered
options.why: This answer confuses the volume injected with the volume the drug behaves as if it occupied. The injected volume is a property of the preparation, and changing the syringe volume would not change the concentration achieved. The volume of distribution is derived from the dose and the resulting plasma concentration, never from the formulation.

list: VD (apparent volume of distribution) answers one question: how large a volume would hold the whole dose at the concentration measured in plasma?
VD = {{frac:D0|C0}}, the dose divided by the plasma concentration at time zero.
If drug leaves the plasma for tissue, the measured plasma concentration is low, so the implied volume is large.
Nothing requires that volume to match an anatomical space, so it can exceed total body water; that is why it is called hypothetical and apparent.

qs.quote: The volume of distribution is a hypothetical volume of body fluid that would be required to dissolve the total amount of drug at the same concentration as that found in the blood.

qs.stem: The volume of distribution acts as a proportionality constant. Which two quantities does it relate?

options.t: The amount in the body and the plasma concentration
options.why: The slide calls it a proportionality constant relating the amount of drug in the body to the measured concentration in the biological fluid, and the relationship is written Cp = {{frac:DB|VD}}. Because it is a constant, the same value converts amount to concentration at any time after the dose, not only at time zero.

options.t: The dose and the elimination rate constant
options.why: Dose and elimination rate constant are independent of each other in a linear first-order system, so no constant links them. Choosing this pairs the volume of distribution with k because the two sit side by side in the clearance equation, and assumes the pairing runs the other way.

options.t: The plasma concentration and the elimination half-life
options.why: For a first-order process the half-life is the same at every concentration, so there is no proportionality between them to describe. That independence is one of the defining properties of first-order elimination, which makes this the exact opposite of a proportional relationship.

options.t: The clearance and the area under the curve
options.why: Clearance and area under the curve are related, but through the dose, as Cl = {{frac:D0|AUC}}, and the constant of proportionality there is the dose rather than the volume of distribution. Placing the volume of distribution in that relationship mixes up the two things clearance is liked for.

list: Calling VD (apparent volume of distribution) a proportionality constant is a statement about arithmetic, not anatomy.
The amount in the body and the plasma concentration are two readings of the same drug: amount = concentration × VD, and concentration = amount ÷ VD.
VD does not change with time, so either reading converts to the other at any point on the curve.
At time zero the amount is the whole dose, so VD = {{frac:D0|C0}}.

qs.quote: we are talking about the volume distribution being a proportionality constant which relates the amount of drug into the in the body to whatever concentration we measure.

qs.stem: Which parameter describes the elimination of drug in terms of the volume of fluid cleared of drug per unit time?

options.t: Clearance
options.why: Clearance is the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time. It measures drug elimination from the body without identifying the mechanism or process, so it can be quoted for the whole body without separating metabolism from excretion. Dr. Mosley repeats this definition almost word for word in the exam review.

options.t: Excretion
options.why: Excretion names one route of loss, the removal of intact drug or metabolite, rather than a rate parameter with units. It answers where the drug goes, not how much volume is stripped of it per hour, so it cannot be the quantity the units describe.

options.t: Elimination rate
options.why: Picking this reads an amount per unit time as a volume per unit time. An elimination rate is milligrams per hour, and for a first-order drug it falls as the concentration falls. Clearance is the volume of plasma stripped of drug per hour and stays constant; multiplying clearance by the current concentration gives the rate.

options.t: Biotransformation
options.why: Biotransformation is the chemical conversion of the drug to another species, so it is a process rather than a measurement. It contributes to clearance through hepatic metabolism, but it carries no volume-per-time meaning of its own.

list: Clearance (Cl) is the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time. It names no mechanism, so it can describe the whole body at once.
Its units are volume per time, such as L/hr: how much fluid is completely cleared each hour, not how many milligrams leave.
The amount leaving per hour is the elimination rate, Cl × Cp, where Cp is the plasma concentration.
Cl = k × VD (k the elimination rate constant, VD the apparent volume of distribution); this one is not on the equation sheet. Also Cl = {{frac:D0|AUC}}.

qs.quote: Volume of plasma that is cleared of drug per unit time

qs.stem: Which of the following is true about the total body clearance of a drug that follows first-order kinetics?

options.t: It is the product of k and the volume of distribution
options.why: Both k and VD are constants for a given drug in a given patient, so their product is a constant too. Dr. Mosley makes exactly that argument: a constant times a constant is a constant, which is the reason clearance is used as a parameter at all.

options.t: It increases in proportion to the plasma concentration present
options.why: The statement is false. Changing the concentration changes the rate of elimination in milligrams per hour, but the volume stripped per hour is unchanged. Selecting this confuses the rate with the clearance, which is the single most common error on this parameter.

options.t: It is expressed in units of volume rather than volume per time
options.why: Picking this reads clearance as a volume, like VD (apparent volume of distribution). Clearance is volume per unit time, usually litres per hour, and the per-hour is not optional: a quantity in plain litres is a volume of distribution. Dropping the time from the units collapses the two parameters into each other.

options.t: It is the amount of drug eliminated per unit time
options.why: This answer confuses clearance with the elimination rate, the neighbouring term she contrasts with it. The amount eliminated per unit time, in milligrams per hour, is clearance multiplied by the plasma concentration, so it falls as the concentration falls. Clearance, the volume of plasma cleared per hour, stays constant while that rate changes.

list: Clearance (Cl) is valued because it stays constant while the plasma concentration, and the milligrams removed per hour, fall.
Two routes reach it: multiply the two constants, Cl = k × VD, or divide the dose by the AUC (area under the whole curve), Cl = {{frac:D0|AUC}}.
Both routes give the same number, in volume per unit time. Cl = k × VD is not on the equation sheet.
Doubling the dose leaves clearance and half-life unchanged and doubles the initial concentration.

qs.quote: what we like about clearance is that clearance. For most drugs in most situations, it is going to be a constant … a constant times a constant is a constant.

qs.stem: Why do some drugs require a multicompartment rather than a one-compartment model?

options.t: They reach different tissues at different rates
options.why: Some drugs distribute at different rates into different tissue groups. Dr. Mosley describes the drug going to some organs first, before it is distributed uniformly through the body. The one-compartment assumption of instantaneous uniform distribution cannot represent that.

options.t: They are eliminated by more than one route
options.why: Picking this reads a second elimination route as a second compartment. Multiple routes are handled inside the one-compartment model, where k, the overall elimination rate constant, is the sum of km (metabolism) and ke (excretion). Adding a route changes k but not the shape of the plasma curve, so it cannot force a second compartment.

options.t: They follow zero-order rather than first-order elimination
options.why: This answer confuses kinetic order with compartment count, two separate questions. A zero-order decline is a straight line on linear axes and a curve on logarithmic axes; the two-compartment signature is a curve that is biphasic on logarithmic axes while remaining first order throughout. Neither description depends on the other.

options.t: They are given by a route other than intravenous bolus
options.why: Picking this reads the compartment count as a property of the route. The multicompartment material in this module is taught for intravenous bolus administration, so the route cannot be what distinguishes it. A different route changes only the input function; the number of compartments is fixed by how fast the drug reaches its tissues.

list: The number of compartments is decided by the shape of the plasma curve, which reflects how quickly the drug reaches its various tissues.
If everything equilibrates fast enough to look instantaneous, one compartment is enough.
If some tissues take up drug measurably more slowly, the plasma concentration falls steeply at first as drug moves into them, then more gently once that distribution is complete.
Two compartments are needed to describe those two slopes; on a semi-logarithmic plot one straight line means one compartment and a bend means two.
Perfusion is blood supply: the most perfused organs, such as the heart, liver and kidney, take up the drug first; the brain is highly perfused but sits behind the blood–brain barrier.

qs.quote: Multi-compartment models describe the observation of some drugs that distribute at various rates into different tissue groups

qs.stem: A plasma concentration-versus-time curve after an intravenous bolus dose is plotted on a logarithmic concentration scale. The curve has a steep initial segment that then bends into a shallower straight segment. What does that shape indicate?

options.t: A two-compartment model
options.why: On a logarithmic scale a one-compartment first-order decline is one straight line. A steep segment bending into a shallower line has two slopes: two processes with different rate constants, the first being distribution into the tissue compartment. Dr. Mosley gives this as a graph-reading rule for the exam.

options.t: A one-compartment model
options.why: A one-compartment model gives one straight line on a logarithmic scale, not a bend, because a single first-order process has a single slope. Choosing this usually means reading the shallow later segment on its own and ignoring the steep segment that precedes it.

options.t: A zero-order elimination process
options.why: Picking this reads a bend on a logarithmic plot as a change of kinetic order. Zero-order elimination is a straight line on a linear scale and a smooth curve on a logarithmic one, never a two-slope bend. Both segments here are straight on the log scale, so both are first order with different rate constants.

options.t: A drug given by oral administration
options.why: This answer confuses the two-slope bend with the rise and fall of an oral curve. An oral curve rises to a peak before falling, because absorption competes with elimination at early times. The curve here starts at its maximum and only falls, which identifies the input as a bolus; the bend is distribution, not absorption.

list: Check the axis before reading the line.
On a logarithmic concentration scale, the number of straight segments equals the number of exponential terms in the equation.
One segment: one compartment and one rate constant.
Two segments joined by a bend: two exponential terms, a fast one for distribution and a slow one for elimination. The model needs two compartments.

qs.cite: Basic Pharmacokinetics - 08-26 Lecture.txt (exam cue on graph reading)
qs.quote: if I give you a graph that looks something like this without the red and blue and just a log scale and I am telling you that it is an IV bolus dose … That should say to you that this is a two compartment model.
qs.note: On the exam the axis may not say that it is logarithmic. Values that go up by a factor of 10 at each gridline (1, 10, 100) mark a log scale.
qs.audit: The deck slide "Why Multicompartment Models?" plots log Cp against time without labelling the scale as logarithmic. Dr. Mosley supplies the reading rule out loud and repeats it in the exam review, so the rule is taken from the transcript. An exam written from these lectures would expect the scale to be inferred from the axis values.

qs.stem: In the two-compartment open model for intravenous bolus injection, with a central and a tissue compartment, from which compartment is drug eliminated?

options.t: From the central compartment only
options.why: The model diagram puts the elimination rate constant k on the central compartment, with k12 and k21 moving drug back and forth between central and tissue compartments. Dr. Mosley describes drug equilibrating with the peripheral compartment while being eliminated from the central one only, the version used most of the time.

options.t: From the tissue compartment only
options.why: The slide showing examples of two-compartment models does include a variant with elimination from the tissue compartment, but it is not the one this course uses. Choosing it puts the exit on the wrong side of the diagram, which changes the differential equations and every rate-constant expression that follows.

options.t: From both compartments at equal rates
options.why: Equal elimination from both compartments would collapse the distinction between them, since the two would then differ only in their transfer constants. The model is built precisely so that one compartment is the site of both measurement and elimination.

options.t: From whichever compartment holds the higher concentration
options.why: This answer confuses the rates in the model with its structure. Elimination is fixed where the model is drawn, with the rate constant k on the central compartment, and does not move with the concentrations. The concentrations set the transfer rates k12·Cp and k21·Ct and the elimination rate k·Cp, not where the exit is.

list: The two-compartment open model has three arrows.
k12: drug moves from the central compartment to the tissue compartment. k21: drug moves back from tissue to central.
k: drug leaves the body, from the central compartment.
k is placed there because the kidney and liver, where excretion and metabolism happen, are highly perfused organs and so belong to the central compartment.
The central compartment is also the one sampled, so plasma concentration reflects elimination directly, and tissue uptake only through its effect on the central concentration.

qs.quote: if we have got a central compartment, it is going to and from that tissue compartment … and then that the drug is being eliminated from the central compartment only.

qs.stem: In the two-compartment open model, which process appears in the central-compartment equation dCp/dt = k21·Ct − k12·Cp − k·Cp but not in the tissue-compartment equation dCt/dt = k12·Cp − k21·Ct?

options.t: Elimination of drug from the body
options.why: The first two terms mirror the tissue equation with the signs reversed: drug returning from tissue is a gain to the central compartment, and drug leaving for tissue a loss. The third term, −k·Cp, has no match because it is drug leaving the body, which happens only from the central compartment.

options.t: Transfer of drug from the tissue compartment to the central compartment
options.why: Picking this reads the gain term k21·Ct as something only the central compartment sees. Transfer from tissue to central appears in both equations: as +k21·Ct in the central equation, a gain, and as −k21·Ct in the tissue equation, a loss. What leaves one compartment arrives in the other, so the term is shared.

options.t: Input of the bolus dose
options.why: Picking this reads the dose as a term that must appear in the equations. A bolus is instantaneous, so it enters as the initial condition, Cp at time zero, rather than as a term in the differential equation. Continuing input terms belong to infusion and oral models, where drug keeps arriving; neither equation has one.

options.t: Binding of drug to plasma proteins
options.why: This answer confuses a process acting on the drug with a term in the model. Protein binding is not represented explicitly; its effect is absorbed into the volumes and the transfer constants k12 and k21. Neither equation distinguishes bound from unbound drug, so binding cannot be the term that only one of them carries.

list: A compartment differential equation is a balance: drug entering the compartment is positive and drug leaving is negative.
The two transfer terms (k12 and k21) appear in both equations with opposite signs, because what leaves one compartment arrives in the other.
The elimination term, −k·Cp, appears only where the exit is: the central compartment.

qs.stem: 250 mg of an antibiotic was administered as an IV bolus injection to a 70-kg patient. The concentration at 4 and 8 hours after administration of the dose was 6.6 mcg/mL and 2.18 mcg/mL, respectively. What is the elimination rate constant?

steps.why: Two concentrations at two times define the slope of the log-linear decline, and the rate constant is that slope with the sign reversed. The earlier and larger concentration goes on top so the logarithm is positive, which is what keeps k from coming out negative.

Dr. Mosley tells the class to take it on her word that micrograms per millilitre equals milligrams per litre, so no arithmetic conversion is needed. Here the units cancel inside the ratio anyway, but the equivalence matters for the later parts that pair a concentration with a dose in milligrams.

The ratio {{frac:6.6|2.18}} is 3.0275 and its natural logarithm is 1.10774. Dividing by the four-hour interval between the samples converts a dimensionless logarithm into a quantity in reciprocal hours.
The quotient is 0.276936, which her key prints as 0.2769 hr⁻¹. She asks for three to four decimal places on k so that early truncation does not shift every downstream answer.

setup.why: "IV bolus injection" with concentrations at two times, so the one-compartment IV bolus block with first-order decline. Given Cp at 4 and 8 hours, asked the "elimination rate constant", so ln C = ln C0 − kt between the two points rearranged to k = {{frac:ln(Cp1 ÷ Cp2)|t2 − t1}}. No hinge.

givens: not needed: k comes from two concentrations alone
the later time; t₂ − t₁ = 4 hr
the numerator of the ratio, as 6.6 mg/L
the denominator of the ratio, as 2.18 mg/L

check.t: From 4 to 8 hr the concentration falls 6.6 → 2.18 mcg/mL, to about a third: more than halved but not quartered in 4 hr, so t½ is between 2 and 4 hr and k between 0.693 over 4 and 0.693 over 2; 0.2769 fits.

list: The two-point slope for k (the elimination rate constant) is the same whether the data come as a table or as two concentrations in a sentence: k = {{frac:ln(C1 ÷ C2)|t2 − t1}}.
The denominator is the difference between the two sampling times, not the time since the dose.
The dose and the body weight are not needed for k.

qs.stem:
The data presented in the table below are plasma concentrations of a new drug at different time points after an intravenous bolus injection of 50 mg to a 70-kg patient.

Time (hr) | Plasma concentration (mg/L)
0.5 | 2.52
1.0 | 1.59
1.5 | 1.00
2.0 | 0.64
2.5 | 0.40
3.0 | 0.25

What is the elimination rate constant?

steps.t: k = −slope = {{frac:ln Cp1 − ln Cp2|t2 − t1}}, taking the 1.0 hr and 2.0 hr points, which is the pair Dr. Mosley works in her own key
steps.why: On semi-logarithmic axes a first-order decline is a straight line with slope −k, so ln of two concentrations over the elapsed time gives k. Her key uses this pair; the concentrations are rounded to two decimals, so other pairs differ slightly. k is never negative, so the minus sign goes on the slope.

The difference of two natural logarithms is the natural logarithm of their ratio, which is the rearrangement she uses because the concentration units cancel inside the ratio and leave a pure number. Dividing that pure number by a time in hours is what produces reciprocal hours.

The ratio {{frac:1.59|0.64}} is 2.4844 and its natural logarithm is 0.91002. Because the two sampling times are exactly one hour apart the division leaves the logarithm unchanged in magnitude and only attaches the reciprocal-hour unit.

Report rate constants to four decimal places. A k rounded early to one or two figures carries a large error into every later part of the problem, and four decimals is the precision her key prints for this one.

setup.why: "intravenous bolus injection" with a table of plasma concentrations, so the one-compartment IV bolus block with first-order decline. Given Cp at two times, asked the "elimination rate constant", so ln C = ln C0 − kt between the two points rearranged to k = {{frac:ln(Cp1 ÷ Cp2)|t2 − t1}}. No hinge.

givens: not needed: k comes from two concentrations alone
the 1.0 hr concentration, in mg/L, the numerator of the ratio
the 2.0 hr concentration, the denominator of the ratio
the later time; t₂ − t₁ = 1.0 hr
not needed: the stem names the 1.0 and 2.0 hr pair

check.t: From 1.0 to 2.0 hr the concentration falls 1.59 → 0.64 mg/L, more than half in one hour, so the half-life is under 1 hr and k is above 0.693 hr⁻¹; 0.91 fits.

list: Every rate constant in this module comes from one operation: k = {{frac:ln(C1 ÷ C2)|t2 − t1}}, the natural log of the ratio of two concentrations divided by the time between them.
Put the earlier concentration on top. The ratio then exceeds one and the log is positive, matching the rule that a rate constant is never negative.
k then feeds the rest of the set: t½ = {{frac:0.693|k}}, the back-extrapolated C0, VD = {{frac:D0|C0}} and Cl = k × VD.

qs.note: Other neighbouring pairs of points in this table give k values from 0.893 to 0.940 hr⁻¹. All of them are accepted: the spread comes from rounding in the printed concentrations, not from a mistake in method.
qs.audit: Her key works the 1.0 hr and 2.0 hr points and prints 0.9100 hr⁻¹. The other adjacent pairs in the same table give 0.893 to 0.940 hr⁻¹, and a least-squares fit through all six points gives 0.922 hr⁻¹, so a student who picked a different pair has not made an error of method; the spread is measurement rounding in the printed concentrations, not a mistake. The tolerance is set wide enough to admit that spread.

qs.stem: After an intravenous bolus injection of 50 mg, a drug with an elimination rate constant of 0.91 hr⁻¹ has a plasma concentration of 0.40 mg/L at 2.5 hours. What is the initial plasma concentration?

steps.why: Going backwards along the curve from a measured point to time zero reverses the sign of the exponent in Cp = Cp0·e^(−kt). Keeping the minus sign gives a number lower than the one you started from, which cannot be right: the initial concentration must be the highest point in the data set.

Reciprocal hours multiplied by hours leaves the exponent dimensionless, which it must be. The 2.5 hr is the full elapsed time from the dose to the sample being extrapolated from, so the whole decline over that interval is undone in one step.
The exponent is 2.275 and e raised to it is 9.7279. Multiplying a concentration by a pure number keeps the concentration unit, so the answer is in milligrams per litre.

Her key prints 3.89 mg/L, three significant figures. The value is higher than the earliest measured concentration of 2.52 mg/L at 0.5 hr, which is the sanity check she asks for: the initial concentration should be the highest point.

setup.why: "intravenous bolus injection" with a rate constant and one sampled concentration, so the one-compartment first-order decline line. Given k, t and Cp, asked the "initial plasma concentration" Cp0, so Cp = Cp0 e^(−kt) rearranged to Cp0 = Cp e^(kt). No hinge.

givens: not needed: the decline is worked in concentration
the sampled concentration, multiplied by e^(kt) = 9.7279
the sample time in the exponent

check.t: With k = 0.91 hr⁻¹ the half-life is about three quarters of an hour, so 2.5 hours is more than three half-lives: Cp0 is more than eight times 0.40 mg/L, and 3.89 mg/L fits.

list: Back-extrapolation to time zero is the forward equation run in reverse, C0 = Ct·e^(+kt). Only the sign of the exponent changes.
Any measured point on the line can be used, because it is the same line.
C0 is the concentration that would have been measured if sampling had been instantaneous.
The extrapolated C0, not the first sample, pairs with the dose to give VD (apparent volume of distribution).

qs.stem: A drug given by intravenous bolus injection has an initial plasma concentration of 3.89 mg/L and an elimination rate constant of 0.91 hr⁻¹. What is the concentration of drug in the plasma 15 minutes after the dose was given?

steps.why: The rate constant is in reciprocal hours, so the time must be in hours before the two are multiplied or the exponent will be sixty times too large. She converts 15 minutes to 0.25 hr silently in her key, but the conversion is the step that decides whether the answer is right.

This is the forward form of the integrated first-order equation, used whenever a concentration at a stated later time is wanted from a known starting concentration. The minus sign belongs here because the concentration is falling.

The exponent is −0.2275, and e raised to it is 0.79652, the fraction of the starting concentration still present. Multiplying the initial concentration by that fraction gives the concentration at 15 minutes.
Her key prints 3.1 mg/L. Since a quarter of an hour is well under one half-life of 0.76 hr, the answer must lie between 3.89 and half of 3.89, which it does.

setup.why: "intravenous bolus injection" with an "initial plasma concentration", so the one-compartment first-order decline line. Given Cp0, k and t, asked Cp, so Cp = Cp0 e^(−kt) directly. The minutes become hours to match k; that is a unit conversion, not a hinge.

givens: the starting concentration, multiplied by e^(−kt)
becomes 0.25 hr so the exponent is a pure number

check.t: A quarter hour is about a third of the half-life of three quarters of an hour, so only about 20 per cent is lost: Cp sits a little under 3.89 mg/L and above half of it, and 3.1 mg/L fits.

list: Before Cp = Cp0·e^(−kt) can be evaluated, the time unit in the exponent must match the time unit in k (the elimination rate constant).
This problem states the interval in minutes while k is per hour, so the minutes must be converted.
Once the exponent has no units, e^(−kt) is the fraction remaining. Multiply it by the starting concentration to finish.

qs.stem: A drug has an apparent volume of distribution of 12.85 L and an elimination rate constant of 0.91 hr⁻¹ in a patient. What is the total body clearance of this drug in this patient?

steps.why: Total body clearance is the product of the overall elimination rate constant and the volume of distribution. This relationship is not supplied on the equation sheet, so it has to be recalled. Both factors are constants, which is why their product is constant too.

Litres multiplied by reciprocal hours gives litres per hour, which is the unit a clearance must carry. A result in plain litres would mean the rate constant had been left out and a volume of distribution reported instead.
Her key prints 11.7 L/hr, three significant figures. Carrying both inputs unrounded, as VD = 12.8535 L and k = 0.91002 hr⁻¹, gives 11.697 L/hr, which rounds to the same value.

setup.why: "total body clearance" from a "volume of distribution" and an "elimination rate constant", so the clearance line. Given k and VD, asked ClT, so ClT = k·VD directly. No hinge.

givens: one factor of the product k · VD

check.t: 0.91 is a little under 1, so k × VD is a little under 12.85 L/hr; 11.7 L/hr fits.

list: Clearance (Cl) is found by multiplying two parameters already in hand: Cl = k × VD. It is not on the equation sheet.
k (the elimination rate constant) is the fraction of the body content that leaves per hour; VD (the apparent volume of distribution) is how large the body content appears to be.
Their product is the volume cleared of drug per hour.
Both inputs are constant for that drug in that patient, so clearance does not change as the concentration falls.

qs.stem: A 187-pound male patient received a drug by rapid IV injection. The drug has a half-life of 4 hours and an apparent volume of distribution that is 20% of body weight. What is the total body clearance in this patient?

steps.why: Body weight in pharmacokinetics is always in kilograms, so a weight stated in pounds is converted before anything else is done with it. She divides by 2.2 and does not show the step, but every absolute quantity in this problem depends on it.

steps.t: ClT = k · VD, so the half-life has to become a rate constant and the percentage of body weight has to become an absolute volume before the two can be multiplied
steps.why: Total body clearance is k multiplied by VD, and neither is given directly: the stem gives a half-life and a percentage. Naming the relation first shows which two quantities have to be built. Dr. Mosley leaves this relation off the exam equation sheet, so it has to be known.

A volume of distribution that is 20% of body weight becomes 0.2 L per kilogram under the assumption that 1 L corresponds to 1 kg. Multiplying by the patient weight in kilograms converts it into the absolute volume that clearance needs.
The clearance equation takes a rate constant, not a half-life, so the stated half-life is converted first. Her keys report k to four decimal places throughout.
Reciprocal hours multiplied by litres gives litres per hour. This is the relationship she withholds from the equation sheet, so both factors have to be assembled before it can be used.
Her key prints 2.95 L/hr, two decimal places. Carrying k unrounded as 0.17325 hr⁻¹ gives 2.9453 L/hr, which rounds to the same value.

setup.why: "rapid IV injection" and "total body clearance", so the clearance line. Given t½ and VD as a per cent of body weight, asked ClT, so ClT = k·VD. k first, from k = {{frac:0.693|t½}}, because the line wants k, not t½; the pounds to kilograms and per cent to litres steps are unit conversions.

givens: the fraction of 85.0 kg that is the volume, 17.0 L

check.t: 187 lb is 85.0 kg, so VD is 17.0 L, and k is 0.693 over 4, 0.1733 hr⁻¹; about a sixth of 17.0 L cleared each hour is a little under 3 L/hr, so 2.95 L/hr fits.

list: With the weight in pounds, a clearance question has three steps before the final product.
First, convert the weight to kilograms by dividing by 2.2.
Second, turn the percent-of-body-weight volume into an absolute volume in litres, taking 1 kg as 1 L.
Third, convert the half-life into a rate constant: k = {{frac:0.693|t½}}.
Only then does Cl = k·VD apply. Skipping any one step changes the answer by a whole factor, not by a rounding.

qs.stem: A 50 mg intravenous bolus dose produces an initial plasma concentration of 3.89 mg/L in a 70-kg patient. What is the apparent volume of distribution?

steps.t: VD = {{frac:DB|Cp}}, with DB = D0 at time zero
steps.why: The volume of distribution is the proportionality constant between the amount of drug in the body and the measured plasma concentration, so rearranging Cp = {{frac:DB|VD}} puts the amount on top. Immediately after a bolus the amount in the body is the whole dose, which is what lets the dose be used here.

The milligrams cancel between numerator and denominator and the litre in the denominator of the concentration inverts, leaving litres. That unit check is also the apples-to-apples check she insists on: an amount is divided by a concentration, never by another amount.
Her key prints 12.85 L, two decimal places. The patient weight of 70 kg is given in the stem and is not used, which is a habit of hers in these problems.

setup.why: "intravenous bolus dose" with an "initial plasma concentration", so the one-compartment block at time zero. Given D0 and Cp0, asked the "apparent volume of distribution", so Cp = {{frac:DB|VD}} with DB = D0 at time zero, rearranged to VD = {{frac:D0|Cp0}}. No hinge.

givens: the numerator: the amount in the body at time zero
not needed: VD comes from the dose and the concentration

check.t: 50 mg over 4 mg/L would be near 12 L, and 3.89 is a little under 4, so VD is a little over 12 L; 12.85 L fits, roughly a fifth of the 70-kg body weight.

list: VD (apparent volume of distribution) is always the amount in the body divided by the concentration at the same instant.
Time zero is the convenient instant: the amount is the whole dose, and the concentration is the back-extrapolated initial value.
Dividing the full dose by a later measured concentration pairs an amount from one time with a concentration from another.

qs.stem: A 250-mg IV bolus dose of a drug is described by A = 8.45 mg/L, B = 5.32 mg/L, α = 2.18 hr⁻¹ and β = 0.114 hr⁻¹. What is the overall elimination rate constant k?

steps.why: The overall elimination rate constant of the two-compartment model is a composite of both intercepts and both exponents, and this expression is printed on the supplied equation sheet. It is not the same quantity as beta, which is the terminal slope of the plasma curve.

The two rate constants multiply to 0.248520 in units of reciprocal hours squared, and the sum of the intercepts is 13.77 mg/L. Multiplying them gives a quantity in mg/L per hour squared, which the denominator will reduce.

Each intercept is paired with the exponent of the other phase, which is what makes this a cross product rather than a simple sum. The result is in mg/L per hour, so dividing the numerator by it leaves reciprocal hours.
The division cancels the concentration units entirely and leaves one power of reciprocal time, which is what a first-order rate constant must carry.
Report 0.272 per hour, to three decimal places. k is larger than beta, as it always is, because beta is slowed by drug returning from the tissue compartment.

setup.why: "IV bolus dose" described by A, B, α and β, so the two-compartment block. Given the two intercepts and two slopes, asked the "overall elimination rate constant k", so k = (A + B)αβ ÷ (Aβ + Bα) directly. No hinge.

givens: not needed: k comes from the intercepts and slopes
in A + B = 13.77 and in Aβ
in A + B and in Bα

check.t: The overall k always lies between the two slopes, above β = 0.114 hr⁻¹ and below α = 2.18 hr⁻¹, and 0.272 does; it sits nearer β because most of the decline follows the slow slope.

list: The overall rate constant k and the terminal slope beta are different numbers, and the model needs both.
Beta is how fast the plasma concentration actually falls once distribution is over. It is slowed by drug coming back out of tissue.
The overall k is elimination from the central compartment itself, which is why it is always the larger of the two.
The elimination half-life still comes from beta, not from k.

qs.cite: 2IVBolusAdministration.pdf, slide "Rate Constants"; in-class two-compartment practice sheet problem 1, answers read aloud in Basic Pharmacokinetics - 08-26 Lecture.txt
qs.quote: I got for the overall rate constant K 0.272 per hour.
qs.audit: The A, B, alpha and beta values for this practice sheet appear on this copy of the deck as handwriting, which is not on its own a source. They are used here only because every answer Dr. Mosley reads aloud in the 26 August lecture reproduces from them exactly: beta half-life six-ish hours, initial concentration 13.8 mg/L, concentration at 4 hours 3.4 mg/L, central volume 18-ish litres, k 0.272 per hour, k12 1.1 per hour and k21 0.9 per hour.

qs.stem: A 300-mg IV bolus dose of a drug was administered to six healthy volunteers. The parameters below best describe the pharmacokinetics of the drug: A = 10.21 mg/L, B = 8.53 mg/L, α = 3.14 hr⁻¹, β = 0.198 hr⁻¹. What is the elimination half-life in these volunteers?

steps.why: Beta is the elimination rate constant for a two-compartment drug, so the half-life relationship applies to it directly. The larger exponent alpha belongs to the distribution phase and is not used here.

Dividing the dimensionless 0.693 by a rate constant in reciprocal hours leaves hours. No other parameter from the stem enters, which is why she instructs students not to solve for the overall k first.
Her key prints 3.5 hr, one decimal place. Half-life must be reported in units of time, never in reciprocal time.

setup.why: "IV bolus dose" described by "A", "B", "α" and "β", so the two-compartment block. Given β, asked the "elimination half-life", so t½β = {{frac:0.693|β}} directly. No hinge.

givens: not needed: the half-life comes from β alone
not needed: the fast slope describes distribution, not elimination

check.t: 0.693 over 0.198 is 0.693 over about a fifth, about 3.5 hr. The elimination half-life comes from β, the smaller slope, so it must be longer than 0.693 over 3.14, under a quarter hour.

list: A two-compartment problem often gives four parameters when only one is needed.
Sort them by unit: the two in reciprocal time are rate constants, and the two in concentration are intercepts.
The smaller rate constant is elimination (beta), and the elimination half-life, {{frac:0.693|beta}}, follows in one division.
An unqualified "half-life" in a two-compartment problem means the beta half-life. The intercepts and the dose belong to other parts of the problem.

qs.stem:
2. The equation below represents the concentration of drug in the plasma following IV bolus administration of a 350 mg bolus dose. (Concentration is given in mcg/mL and time in hours)

Cp = 8.72e^(−3.85t) + 5.40e^(−0.154t)

a. What is the elimination half-life of this agent?

steps.why: The elimination phase is the smaller exponent, β; the larger, α, is distribution and is not the half-life asked for.

list: Cp = A e^(−αt) + B e^(−βt); α is the larger exponent (distribution), β the smaller (elimination).
Elimination half-life t½β = {{frac:0.693|β}}.
At t = 0 both exponentials are 1, so Cp0 = A + B.
Volume of the central compartment Vp = {{frac:D0|A + B}}.

qs.note: Her homework wording with different numbers, so this is not the graded answer.

setup.why: The stem gives a two-exponential equation for "IV bolus administration", so the two-compartment block. α and β are read from the equation and "the elimination half-life" is asked, so t½β = {{frac:0.693|β}}, the beta half-life line, using the smaller exponent.

givens: not needed: half-life does not depend on the dose
not needed: an intercept, not a rate
not needed: the larger exponent is distribution

check.t: β = 0.154 hr⁻¹ removes about 14% an hour, so halving takes between 4 and 5 hours: 4.50 hr. The α term, with a half-life well under an hour, is gone long before.

qs.stem:
2. The equation below represents the concentration of drug in the plasma following IV bolus administration of a 350 mg bolus dose. (Concentration is given in mcg/mL and time in hours)

Cp = 8.72e^(−3.85t) + 5.40e^(−0.154t)

b. What is the initial concentration of drug in the plasma upon administration of the dose?

steps.why: Cp = A e^(−αt) + B e^(−βt) gives the concentration at any time; at t = 0 both exponents are zero and e^0 = 1, so each term equals its intercept and Cp0 = A + B = 8.72 + 5.40 = 14.12 mcg/mL, the concentration the moment the 350 mg bolus is in.

list: Cp = A e^(−αt) + B e^(−βt); α is the larger exponent (distribution), β the smaller (elimination).
Elimination half-life t½β = {{frac:0.693|β}}.
At t = 0 both exponentials are 1, so Cp0 = A + B.
Volume of the central compartment Vp = {{frac:D0|A + B}}.

qs.note: Her homework wording with different numbers, so this is not the graded answer.

setup.why: Two-compartment "IV bolus" equation. A and B are read from the equation and "the initial concentration" is asked, so Cp0 = A + B, the two-compartment time-zero line, because both exponentials equal 1 at t = 0.

givens: not needed: the intercepts already carry the dose
not needed: at t = 0 both exponentials equal 1
not needed: at t = 0 both exponentials equal 1

check.t: At time zero both exponentials are 1, so Cp0 is the plain sum 8.72 + 5.40 = 14.12 mcg/mL, above either intercept alone.

qs.stem:
2. The equation below represents the concentration of drug in the plasma following IV bolus administration of a 350 mg bolus dose. (Concentration is given in mcg/mL and time in hours)

Cp = 8.72e^(−3.85t) + 5.40e^(−0.154t)

c. What is the concentration of drug in the plasma 4 hours after administration of the dose?

steps.why: The two-compartment equation Cp = A e^(−αt) + B e^(−βt) holds at any time, so both terms are evaluated at t = 4 hr. α = 3.85 hr⁻¹ is the distribution rate constant and β = 0.154 hr⁻¹ the elimination rate constant; each exponent is hr⁻¹ times hours, a pure number: 15.4 and 0.616.
By 4 hours the distribution term is almost gone, so the elimination term carries nearly all the concentration.

list: Cp = A e^(−αt) + B e^(−βt); α is the larger exponent (distribution), β the smaller (elimination).
Elimination half-life t½β = {{frac:0.693|β}}.
At t = 0 both exponentials are 1, so Cp0 = A + B.
Volume of the central compartment Vp = {{frac:D0|A + B}}.

qs.note: Her homework wording with different numbers, so this is not the graded answer.

setup.why: Two-compartment "IV bolus" equation. A, α, B and β are read from the equation and the concentration "4 hours after administration" is asked, so Cp = Ae^(−αt) + Be^(−βt) is evaluated at t = 4 hr.

check.t: By 4 hours the α term, e^(−15.4), is zero to five decimals, so only the B term is left; βt = 0.616 is a bit under 0.693, so a bit over half of 5.40 remains: 2.92 mcg/mL, below 5.40.

qs.stem:
2. The equation below represents the concentration of drug in the plasma following IV bolus administration of a 350 mg bolus dose. (Concentration is given in mcg/mL and time in hours)

Cp = 8.72e^(−3.85t) + 5.40e^(−0.154t)

d. What is the apparent volume of distribution of the central compartment? (Part b: Cp0 = 14.12 mcg/mL.)

steps.why: The central compartment is the volume the dose first distributes into, so Vp = {{frac:D0|Cp0}} with Cp0 = A + B = 14.12 mcg/mL, the concentration at time zero. 1 mcg/mL equals 1 mg/L, so 350 mg over 14.12 mg/L cancels the milligrams and leaves litres, 24.79 L.

list: Cp = A e^(−αt) + B e^(−βt); α is the larger exponent (distribution), β the smaller (elimination).
Elimination half-life t½β = {{frac:0.693|β}}.
At t = 0 both exponentials are 1, so Cp0 = A + B.
Volume of the central compartment Vp = {{frac:D0|A + B}}.

qs.note: Her homework wording with different numbers, so this is not the graded answer.

setup.why: Two-compartment "IV bolus" of a stated "bolus dose" in mg. The dose and the intercepts A and B are known and "the apparent volume of distribution of the central compartment" is asked, so Vp = {{frac:D0|A + B}}, the central volume from the intercepts.

givens: added to A for Cp0 = 14.12 mg/L in part b, the denominator

check.t: 350 mg producing 14.12 mg/L at time zero fills {{frac:350|14.12}}, about 25 L: 24.79 L, above zero.
